newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking truckers maintain stranglehold on France.
newsitem.headline: Striking truckers maintain stranglehold on France.

text.p: Striking truck drivers maintained their 11-day-old stranglehold on the French economy on Thursday, defying government pleas to return to work after talks with bosses collapsed over pay demands.

Truckers maintained almost 250 barricades on main roads and tightened a blockade of the oil industry after talks foundered around midnight. Employers, crippled by the strike, said their rejected pay offer was "flexible".

The strike forced increasing petrol rationing, shut factories for lack of supplies and trapped hundreds of foreign trucks. But the strikers relaxed a blockade at the Channel port of Calais and let stranded British trucks embark on ferries for home.

The strike, ratified by ballots of strikers camped in trucks parked on chilly highways, defied assurances by Transport Minister Bernard Pons that the main demands on pensions and working hours had been met.
"Perhaps the truckers don't have a good perception of reality," Pons told a news conference at which he urged strikers to resume work. "In a compromise, you can't get everything you want."
"Very positive results were obtained," he said, pointing to accords to cut the retirement age to 55 from 60 and to improve conditions on working hours and sick pay.

Major unions said grassroots members consulted about the talks overwhelmingly voted to continue the strike even though Pons said government mediator Robert Cros had successfully completed his mission.
Road haulage employers said on Thursday their pay offer was open to amendment and urged truckers to end their blockade.

Asked if employers might make a fresh offer, Jean-Louis Amato, president of the Unostra hauliers' association, told a news conference the offer of a one percent real pay rise and a 1,500 franc ($300) one-time bonus was "flexible".
Unions are demanding pay increases that amount to an average 23 percent. "We have made a big effort," said Rene Petit, speaking on behalf of the four employers' federations.
Despite the deadlock on pay, unions and employers are to meet on Friday morning to sign protocols for retirement at 55 after 25 years at the wheel and deals on working time.
Pons ruled out using force to clear the truckers' roadblocks on highways, at ports, borders, refineries and fuel depots.
He said a group made up of representatives of unions and employers would try to tackle the issue of defining working hours for drivers.

"If this working group does not agree quickly, I will propose to the government that we settle the issue by decree," he said. Drivers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid waiting for loading and unloading.
The state traffic information centre counted 245 blockades on major highways at 5 p.m. (1600 GMT) on Thursday, slightly down from 247 on Wednesday. Snow and sleet fell overnight in some areas.

Strikers completed a blockade of oil refineries, forming barricades outside the only one of 13 that had escaped the strike so far. About 5,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages, an industry ministry official said.

The roadblocks have forced closure of some factories and cut supplies of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers. Farmers reported shortages of animal feed as grain shipments were hit. The strike was also disrupting mail.
The French strike and an unrelated truckers' strike in Denmark caused problems in other European countries, clogging highways and ports and disrupting commerce.
